content: Willowbrook State School was a state-funded institution located in central Staten Island, New York City, designed to care for children with intellectual disabilities. The facility became infamous in the 1960s due to an unethical medical study conducted on its grounds. In the 1970s, further abuses were uncovered, which led to significant civil rights reforms. The school was ultimately closed in 1987, and its grounds were extensively redeveloped to serve as the campus for the College of Staten Island. Construction of the facility was completed in 1942, but instead of opening for its intended purpose, it was repurposed as a United States Army hospital named Halloran General Hospital, in honor of Colonel Paul Stacey Halloran. After World War II, there were proposals to transfer the site to the Veterans Administration. However, in October 1947, the New York State Department of Mental Hygiene opened the facility as originally planned, naming it Willowbrook State School. During its first decade of operation, the school experienced frequent outbreaks of hepatitis. Between 1963 and 1966, a highly controversial medical study was conducted at the institution. In this study, healthy children were deliberately infected with the hepatitis virus, both orally and via injection, to study the effects of gamma globulin in combating the disease. Public outrage eventually forced the discontinuation of the study. In early 1972, investigative reporter Geraldo Rivera conducted a series of exposés on the institution, revealing appalling conditions, including severe overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, and physical and sexual abuse of residents by staff members. These revelations led to a class-action lawsuit against the State of New York, filed in federal court on March 17, 1972. A settlement was reached on May 5, 1975, mandating reforms at the facility. However, it took several years to address all the violations. The publicity surrounding the case played a significant role in the passage of the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act in 1980. In 1975, the Willowbrook Consent Decree was signed, committing New York State to improve community placement for the residents, who were now referred to as the Willowbrook class. In 1983, the state announced plans to close the institution, which had been renamed the Staten Island Developmental Center in 1974. By March 1986, the number of residents had decreased to 250, down from a peak of 5,000 during the height of the scandal. The last children left the facility on September 17, 1987. After the developmental center closed, the future of the property became a topic of intense local debate. In 1989, a portion of the land was acquired by the City of New York to establish a new campus for the College of Staten Island. The new campus opened in 1993, coinciding with the closure of one of the college's other campuses in the Sunnyside neighborhood, which was repurposed as a high school. The new campus, spanning 204 acres, is the largest maintained by the City University of New York. However, 171 acres of the original Willowbrook property remain under the administration of the New York State Department of Mental Hygiene, which operates a facility there called the Institute for Basic Research. On February 25, 1987, the Federal Court approved the 1987 Stipulation, which established guidelines for the Office of Mental Retardation and Developmental Disabilities (OMRDD) to ensure community placement for members of the Willowbrook Class.
